TE1-F-01.hint: Write the angle as a sum or difference of two special angles. Then use \(\sin(A \pm B) = \sin A\cos B \pm \cos A\sin B\) or \(\cos(A \pm B) = \cos A\cos B \mp \sin A\sin B\), and substitute exact values.
slips: Using the wrong sign in the cosine formula. \(\cos(A + B)\) has a minus sign and \(\cos(A - B)\) has a plus sign.
Distributing the function: \(\sin(A + B)\) is not \(\sin A + \sin B\).
Dropping a negative sign when substituting values from Quadrants II, III, or IV.

TE1-F-02.hint: Use \(\sin^{2}\theta + \cos^{2}\theta = 1\) (or \(1 + \tan^{2}\theta = \sec^{2}\theta\)) to find the size of the missing value. The quadrant then decides its sign.
slips: Choosing the sign without using the quadrant, or taking only the positive root.
Using the wrong sign for a quadrant. Sine is positive in Quadrants I and II, and cosine is positive in Quadrants I and IV.
Squaring a fraction incorrectly, such as \(\left(\dfrac{3}{5}\right)^{2} = \dfrac{9}{5}\).

TE1-F-03.hint: Replace \(\sin^{2}u\) with \(\dfrac{1 - \cos 2u}{2}\) and \(\cos^{2}u\) with \(\dfrac{1 + \cos 2u}{2}\). The angle inside the cosine doubles. Then multiply the constant through.
slips: Forgetting to double the angle inside the cosine.
Using a plus sign for \(\sin^{2}u\). The sine formula has a minus sign.
Multiplying the constant by only part of the result.

TE1-F-04.hint: Write the angle as half of a special angle \(\theta\). Use \(\sin\dfrac{\theta}{2} = \pm\sqrt{\dfrac{1 - \cos\theta}{2}}\), \(\cos\dfrac{\theta}{2} = \pm\sqrt{\dfrac{1 + \cos\theta}{2}}\), or \(\tan\dfrac{\theta}{2} = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{1 + \cos\theta}\). Choose the sign from the quadrant of \(\dfrac{\theta}{2}\), not of \(\theta\).
slips: Choosing the sign from the quadrant of \(\theta\) instead of the quadrant of \(\dfrac{\theta}{2}\).
Mixing up the plus and minus inside the radical for sine and cosine.
Halving the cosine value instead of halving the angle.

TE1-A-01.hint: Find the missing sine or cosine with the Pythagorean identity, using the quadrant for the sign. Then use \(\sin 2\theta = 2\sin\theta\cos\theta\), \(\cos 2\theta = \cos^{2}\theta - \sin^{2}\theta\), and \(\tan 2\theta = \dfrac{\sin 2\theta}{\cos 2\theta}\).
slips: Computing \(\sin 2\theta\) as \(2\sin\theta\), which doubles the sine instead of using the formula.
Writing \(\cos 2\theta\) as \(\sin^{2}\theta - \cos^{2}\theta\), which has the wrong sign.
Choosing the wrong sign for the missing value because the quadrant was not used.

TE1-A-02.hint: Treat the fourth power as the square of a square. Reduce the inner square, expand the result, and reduce the new \(\cos^{2}\) term. Collect like terms.
slips: Squaring only the first term when expanding, such as \((1 + \cos 2u)^{2} = 1 + \cos^{2}2u\). The middle term \(2\cos 2u\) is lost.
Forgetting to double the angle again in the second reduction.

If \(\sin\theta = -\dfrac{4}{5}\) and \(\theta\) is in Quadrant IV, find \(\cos\theta\).
parts.a: \(\sin^{2}\theta + \cos^{2}\theta = 1\), so \(\cos^{2}\theta = 1 - \left(-\dfrac{4}{5}\right)^{2} = \dfrac{9}{25}\). Then \(\cos\theta = \pm \dfrac{3}{5}\). In Quadrant IV, the cosine is positive. So \(\cos\theta = \dfrac{3}{5}\).

parts.q: If \(\tan\theta = \dfrac{5}{12}\) and \(\theta\) is in Quadrant I, find \(\cos\theta\).
parts.a: \(1 + \tan^{2}\theta = \sec^{2}\theta\), so \(\sec^{2}\theta = 1 + \left(\dfrac{5}{12}\right)^{2} = \dfrac{169}{144}\) and \(\cos\theta = \pm \dfrac{12}{13}\). In Quadrant I, the cosine is positive, so \(\cos\theta = \dfrac{12}{13}\).
